Radar absorbing materials (RAM) have low thermal conductivity (0.5 W/m·K) and high specific heat (1200 J/kg·K).
Aluminum metal has high thermal conductivity (205 W/m·K) and lower specific heat (900 J/kg·K).
Under a 200 W/m² heat flux, RAM surfaces develop a central hotspot with max temperature ~40.19°C.
Metal surfaces stabilize faster (~1.5 seconds) at a lower max temperature (~34.05°C).
RAM surfaces exhibit a surface temperature standard deviation of 3.47°C, indicating high thermal non-uniformity.
Metal surfaces have a surface temperature standard deviation of 0.88°C, indicating uniform heat distribution.
Thermal inertia of RAM causes delayed heat diffusion and longer saturation time (~3.5 seconds) compared to metal.
MuSES thermal simulation software was used with 0.1-second time resolution over 10 seconds.
Infrared image simulations show RAM surfaces have wider brightness distributions and higher IR contrast.
Three integrated design strategies proposed: local thermal control, hierarchical thermal diffusion layers, and thermal inertia distribution optimization.
Local thermal control can use Peltier elements or fluid circulation modules for real-time temperature adjustment.
Hierarchical layers using carbon composites or metal foams can mediate heat transfer between RAM and metal.
Thermal inertia optimization involves varying RAM thickness or density spatially to reduce IR hotspots.
RAM is essential for radar stealth but creates challenges for IR stealth due to thermal properties.
Effective multispectral stealth requires balancing radar absorption and IR thermal signature control.
Active IR stealth involves real-time surface temperature control to minimize thermal contrast.
IR sensors detect both absolute temperature and temperature contrast with background.
RAM is typically applied as an external coating on metal structures, causing thermal mismatch.
The study used a 300mm x 300mm x 5mm flat plate specimen for simulations.
Side surfaces were insulated; bottom surface had convection boundary conditions (10 W/m²·K, 25°C ambient).
The study highlights the importance of integrated stealth design for future complex sensor environments.
Thermal hotspots on RAM surfaces increase IR detectability risk and complicate stealth integration.
The proposed multilayer structure integrates RAM, thermal diffusion layers, metal substrate, and active control modules.
Simulation results provide quantitative data supporting design trade-offs in multispectral stealth.
